papers.title: HardwareDx: A Foundational Graph Model System for Datacenter Machine Repairs
papers.abstract: The rapid scale-up of AI infrastructure has made datacenter reliability a cornerstone of the cloud business economy. Since hardware failures in hyper-scale AI clusters can stall multi-million dollar training workloads, the downtime of individual machines can cause outsized economic losses. Minimizing machine downtime, therefore, is more important than ever. To address this, we present Hardware Diagnoser (HardwareDx), an AI-driven hardware diagnosis system that applies a graph foundation model approach to automated datacenter maintenance. It allows a single model to diagnose many platforms and accelerate onboarding of new hardware products. Deployed at production scale at Google, HardwareDx yields substantial efficiency gains across diverse compute architectures. Real-world evaluations demonstrate that it reduces production downtime by 18.3% on GPU platforms and 16.1% on TPUs. Furthermore, it significantly accelerates hardware deployment, cutting quality assurance (QA) time by 28.3% for GPUs and 25.1% for TPUs. These results establish HardwareDx as a field-tested solution for maximizing the reliability and cost efficiency of next generation AI fleets.

papers.title: BeFit: Shifting Complexity from Weights to Bernstein Activations for Resource-Constrained Sensing
papers.abstract: Time-series sensing increasingly relies on neural networks, yet deployment on resource-constrained microcontrollers remains challenging. Aggressive model compression can reduce accuracy, while restricting weights to multiplication-free representations introduces further losses. We present BeFit, an end-to-end framework that shifts model capacity from weights to learnable Bernstein polynomial activations. BeFit (i) finds compact Bernstein-activated convolutional neural networks (BeCNNs) through hardware-aware neural architecture search and trains them via knowledge distillation; (ii) projects their weights to multiplication-free codes, freezes the codes, and recovers the resulting accuracy loss through the learnable activations; and (iii) generates model-specific kernels that exploit the projected weights for multiplication-free convolutions. On human activity recognition, BeCNNs are 2.75 percentage points (pp) more accurate on average than ReLU CNNs of identical architecture. On a TI CC3220SF (Cortex-M4), weight projection speeds BeCNNs up by 2.2x on average while losing 0.8 pp, compared with 2.4 pp for ReLU CNNs. Against the MLPerf Tiny DS-CNN reference model running on TensorFlow Lite Micro with CMSIS-NN, the unprojected BeCNN achieves 1.0 pp higher accuracy, 2.2x lower latency, and 6.4x lower flash, while the projected model remains within 1.0 pp of the reference accuracy and runs 5.9x faster. In emulation on a RISC-V core without a hardware multiplier, the instruction-count reduction relative to the DS-CNN increases from 5.2x on the Cortex-M4 to 147x. BeFit also extends to transformers and MLPs, and across all tasks the final models stay within 1.56 pp of their float32 teachers on average.

papers.title: Lodestone: Automated Semantic Discovery of Datacenter Hardware Specialization
papers.abstract: Hardware specialization can improve datacenter efficiency. Unfortunately, identifying computations that justify dedicated hardware is difficult. Existing approaches analyze hot functions, instruction patterns, or overheads such as datacenter tax. They can miss fine-grained computations whose aggregate cost is spread across applications and libraries, especially when different pieces of code obscure the same underlying computation. We observe that seemingly unrelated code regions often perform the same computations, creating specialization opportunities that require semantic reasoning. The rise of agentic AI makes it possible to automate this. However, conventional AI agents cannot efficiently and reliably analyze large scale datacenter software. To unlock this opportunity, we present Lodestone, an agentic framework that automatically discovers hardware specialization opportunities by reasoning about what the executed code computes. First, Lodestone extracts hot control-flow regions from execution traces across workloads and organizes them into compact analysis packages that make large workloads tractable for agents. Second, agents describe what each region computes, merge those that perform the same computation into computational families, and check their semantic correctness in a loop. Third, to verify the discovered family, Lodestone runs every piece of code in a family against a set of reference inputs and outputs on recorded executions. Finally, for selected families, Lodestone proposes hardware, e.g., ISA extensions, near-core units, or detached accelerators, and human experts decide which proposals to develop further. We evaluate Lodestone on 20 workloads across six datacenter workload categories. We simulate 30 discovered families in a cycle-accurate simulator and implement them in RTL. These optimizations speed up the workloads by 12.6% on average and by up to 80.2%.

papers.title: HETEROVLM: Edge Multi-Request Vision-Language Model Serving on a Heterogeneous Versal SoC with AI Engines and Programmable Logic
papers.abstract: Edge devices in vehicles and robots serve concurrent requests with different deadlines to a vision-language model (VLM), each mixing a compute-bound encoder and prefill with a memory-bound decode. GPU serving targets datacenter throughput with per-iteration host scheduling: an urgent request waits for the running iteration, and small-batch decode costs much energy per token. Prior accelerators on Versal AI Engine (AIE) SoCs map one model onto a fixed AIE dataflow graph for one input stream, without decode or request scheduling. HETEROVLM keeps the AIE graph static and makes it schedulable. The AIE array runs the encoder, prefill and attention, and the programmable logic (PL) holds GEMV engines for small decode steps and a scheduler that orders short work units by class and deadline. Concurrent requests share one decode step that reads the weights once. An urgent request preempts at a work-unit boundary, and the paused request resumes from its results in DDR. On an AMD Versal VC1902, text and camera questions get their first tokens in 140 and 303 ms. HETEROVLM decodes a single request 1.3x and 4.0x faster than NVIDIA Tesla T4 and Jetson Orin Nano GPUs, with 61% and 73% of their energy per token, and uses 51% of the energy per token of an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 Ti. The same bitstream serves multiple VLMs by loading their own instruction programs and weights. A demo is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/demo heterovlm-EFM2/.

papers.title: Accelerating Distributed Digital Ising Machines
papers.abstract: Ising machines, dedicated accelerators built around the dynamics of Ising-like spin models, have emerged as a leading platform for combinatorial optimization and probabilistic sampling. The problems that motivate them require millions of spins, far beyond the on-chip capacity of any single device, so a practical Ising machine must distribute its computation across many devices. Prior work reports throughput at a single operating point, leaving the binding resource unidentified and platform crossovers measurable only by experiment; no calibrated cross-platform cost model of distributed Ising machines has been reported, nor have systematic techniques to accelerate their Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) workloads. This work presents a calibrated cost model that decomposes digital Ising sweep time into compute, memory, synchronization, and inter-device communication terms, validated with 4.8% mean error across three GPU generations, FPGA and ASIC up to 1 million spins. Guided by the model, we address each term in turn and propose: (i) a data placement strategy, worth up to 4.2$\times$ speedup; (ii) multi-rate and bounded-staleness schedules that relax the barrier that Gibbs sampling imposes, cutting time-to-solution (TTS) by up to 3.16$\times$ on three benchmarks; and (iii) a phase-offset streaming dataflow that hides boundary exchange behind interior computation whenever a link satisfies a latency-transparency criterion, yielding up to 1.25$\times$/1.74$\times$/2.01$\times$ on an H200 pair, a ZCU106 pair, and a four-board XEM8320 $2{\times}2$ mesh. The streaming dataflow is also implemented on a fabricated four-chip 28 nm ASIC sustaining 28.1 Gflips/s at 4.81 pJ/flip.

papers.title: Inference-Time Scaling in Agentic Hardware Verification Workflows: A Multi-Strategy Characterization Across Protocol Complexity
papers.abstract: Inference-time scaling, allocating more compute during generation rather than pre-training, has demonstrated dramatic quality improvements for LLM reasoning tasks. Its behaviour in structured hardware verification code generation, where outputs must satisfy compiler correctness, protocol semantics, and functional coverage constraints simultaneously, is less understood. We present a systematic, simulator-grounded study of inference-time compute scaling for agentic UVM testbench synthesis targeting AMBA protocol bridges. Four inference strategies---zero-shot (\$0.04), raw-feedback iterative (\$0.81), structured inner-loop (\$0.95), and full dual-loop agentic synthesis (\$1.06)---are evaluated across four AMBA targets (Protocol Complexity Index 11.8--22.6) using the Protocol Verification Completeness (PVC) metric, functional coverage, and a six-class UVM error taxonomy (E1--E6). Our central finding is that structured diagnostic feedback acts as an inference-time compute multiplier: the structured inner loop yields roughly $15\times$ more PVC per inference dollar than raw EDA-tool feedback (marginal efficiency, S1$\to$S2 vs. S0$\to$S1). The mechanism is fault targeting, not token reduction: raw compiler feedback drives the testbench to compile but cannot surface functional protocol faults that leave the code syntactically valid, whereas structured E1--E6 bundles diagnose and resolve them. All outputs are judged by a cycle-accurate Mentor Questa toolchain rather than by model self-assessment; the dual-loop strategy reaches PVC $\geq$ 0.95 with zero scoreboard errors on every target, and the generated environments surfaced a latent RTL bug in two of the four reference designs. These results establish a principled compute-quality trade-off curve for LLM-aided verification environment generation and motivate inference-budget-aware deployment strategies for industrial EDA workflows.

papers.title: ReCIM-HD: A 40 nm On-Device Learning Accelerator with Hyperdimensional Computing via Importance-Based Hybrid Digital-ReRAM CIM
papers.abstract: ReCIM-HD is an on-device learning (ODL) accelerator that integrates gradient-free hyperdimensional computing (HDC) with resistive RAM (ReRAM)-based analog compute-in-memory (CIM). ReCIM-HD introduces three key techniques: (1) ultra-low-power HDC-based edge ODL without costly back-propagation operations; (2) non-volatile ReRAM-based storage for class hypervectors and CIM similarity search, enabling energy-efficient inference and power-gating during idle periods without data loss; and (3) a hybrid digital-analog CIM inference flow that protects a small accuracy-critical subset digitally to preserve accuracy. Additionally, it employs a Kronecker HD encoder (KE) to reduce encoding overhead and a customized instruction set architecture (ISA) to support flexible programmability. Fabricated in 40 nm, ReCIM-HD achieves 44.17 TOPS/W (hybrid mode) and 75.8 TOPS/W (ReRAM CIM mode), delivering up to 20.1x higher energy efficiency than the state-of-the-art accelerator.

papers.title: PULSAR-V: I/O-Aware Post-Update Attestation for RISC-V
papers.abstract: Post-update attestation proves that a device installed the intended firmware, not that the image stayed protected until the report was signed. In a multi-master SoC, a master outside the attested processor can corrupt update-critical memory. In contrast, the firmware identity, lifecycle state, and the CPU's protection evidence remain byte-identical to a healthy device's. We present PULSAR-V, a post-update attestation architecture which binds the authenticated update commit to the effective permissions and immutability of both gates (PMP/EPMP on the CPU, the I/O policy mediating DMA), sampled at the commit and at attestation, the I/O gate latching its own commit-time state in hardware. In a RISC-V SoC prototyped on a ZCU102 FPGA (CV32E40S core with 16 PMP regions, IOPMP-style unit, AXI write guard), a 256-byte write from the board's Arm DMA engine bypasses PMP and corrupts the committed image: every conventional claim stays true, and PULSAR-V rejects the device on its I/O-policy evidence alone. It also rejects an intact device whose policy left the image writable, a verdict no integrity check can reach. The gate and its commit latch cost 436 LUTs, 4.6% of the SoC, and evidence collection takes 43.1k cycles independent of image size, 41x less than re-hashing 16 KiB.

papers.title: Hardware Acceleration of Vision-Language-Action Models with Weight Precision Rising over the Flow Steps
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models such as GR00T control robots through an action head: a diffusion transformer that turns noise into a chunk of actions in a few flow-matching steps. Every step re-reads all of the head's weights from DRAM but applies each weight to only about fifty tokens. Inference is therefore memory-bound, and its latency and energy are largely determined by the total number of transferred weight bits. We show that later flow steps attenuate the quantization errors of earlier steps, so the weight precision of an action head should rise over the steps. With plain per-channel rounding and without calibration or training, widths rising over the steps from 2 to 4 bits preserve the closed-loop success of robot policies. These widths transfer 25% fewer bits than 4-bit weights at every step. However, we show that on Jetson AGX Thor, current GPU kernels cannot exploit this per-step precision due to fixed overheads. We therefore present a programmable accelerator whose latency and energy both scale with the transferred weight bits. It decodes entropy-coded weights for bit-serial sub-arrays at the DRAM rate. Because the width changes per step, a run-time allocator divides these sub-arrays between the linear layers and the attention to balance their workloads. The same sub-arrays are thus capable of running action heads of different families and sizes, as well as a vision-language model. On the DRAM side, a requantizer and an entropy encoder at each bank let one stored 8-bit copy replace the copies of all widths. Simulated with LPDDR5X timing, our RTL implementation runs the GR00T N1.6 action head in 8.02 ms per inference with 2, 3, 3 and 4 bits in its four flow steps. With a copy per width and 50% of Thor's memory bandwidth, the accelerator runs this schedule 1.7x faster than Thor in NVFP4, at 9.1x less energy and equal closed-loop success.

papers.title: Dissecting an Unexplored SASS Control-Code Field: Barrier Exemption and Programmable Warp Priority
papers.abstract: Every instruction in NVIDIA's native GPU ISA (SASS) carries a control code that guides hardware scheduling, and prior work has decoded its known fields to optimize GPU kernels. However, one control-code field remains unexplored: it appears over 500000 times in NVIDIA's closed-source libraries such as cuBLAS and cuDNN, yet nvcc never emits it when compiling user programs. This paper presents the first systematic study of this control-code field across GPU architectures from Volta to Blackwell. Using instruction-level microbenchmarks, we show that the field controls two independent hardware mechanisms: barrier exemption (EXEMPT), which allows instructions blocked by a pending barrier to issue early during the barrier wait, and programmable warp priority (START, TILE, and END), which moves warps across three priority levels in the hardware scheduler. We identify the conditions under which each mechanism improves GPU kernel performance and implement a post-compilation binary optimizer that places these marks directly in compiled binaries without modifying source code or the compiler. Evaluated across six GPUs spanning four architectures, our optimizations speed up representative kernels by up to 31.9%, and the optimizer accelerates production kernels in llama.cpp and vLLM by up to 5.4% and end-to-end LLM inference by up to 3.6%.

papers.title: TechReport: Implementing CHERI in gem5
papers.abstract: Despite countless mitigation efforts, memory safety issues still prevail. The recently discovered security issues in PHP underline this fact. One of the most promising approaches to solving this problem is the concept of Capability Hardware Enhanced RISC Instructions (CHERI). There is a well-developed ecosystem of ISA simulators, compilers, operating systems, and hardware designs that support CHERI. However, the lack of a simulator modeling microarchitectural detail hinders efficient and fast design space exploration for CHERI-enhanced designs means the performance impact of CHERI remains understudied. Therefore, we present gem5-CHERI: a CHERI-enhanced adaptation of the gem5 simulator that can boot the CheriBSD operating system and run custom workloads. The simulator is available open-source on GitHub.

papers.title: Reliable arithmetic circuits using less reliable (sub-digital) logic
papers.abstract: The frequent static failure of CMOS logic gates at ultra-low voltages has historically been perceived as a strict barrier to extreme voltage scaling: this paper introduces a statistical circuit law proving this intuition wrong. We discovered a universal power law connecting gate and circuit static failure probabilities, revealing that circuit failure requires the simultaneous breakdown of an entire gate cluster rather than a single component. Because the required cluster size increases rapidly as voltage drops, low-voltage \textit{sub-digital} logic exhibits surprising inherent resilience to static failure. This insight stems from new theoretical tools we developed to quantify static failure, extending well beyond conventional voltage-margin analysis. Consequently, sub-digital processors could potentially offer a viable, near-term solution to drastically reduce the energy demands of AI.

papers.title: Hypnos: A Dual-Phase End-to-End Platform for Scalable Continual Learning at the Edge
papers.abstract: Continual learning (CL) enables neural networks to adapt to non-stationary data streams by mitigating catastrophic forgetting, offering a path to robust, private, and adaptable edge devices. Yet, porting CL to real-world edge devices remains challenging for two reasons: (i) online operation, where sensor data arrives one sample at a time and the device must adapt on-the-fly, and (ii) the low footprint of edge devices, which makes traditional error backpropagation training prohibitive. Inspired by the brain's wake and sleep cycles, the former for rapid adaptation with minimal resources and the latter for long-term consolidation, we introduce Hypnos, an open-source dual-phase platform for efficient CL at the edge. In the wake phase (e.g., daily operation), Hypnos relies on a low-footprint system-on-chip with a RISC-V microcontroller unit (MCU) targeting efficient inference and supporting lightweight gradient-free prototype updates. In the sleep phase (e.g., night-time charging), where wall-plug energy and larger memory budgets are available, a smart charger performs rehearsal-based gradient updates for consolidation. Deployed on a ZCU104 field-programmable gate array (FPGA) and synthesized in a 28-nm process, Hypnos is benchmarked on the CORe50 NICv2-391 protocol. It sets a new state-of-the-art accuracy of 78.6%-81.6% for edge CL systems, with an on-device latency of 7.79s-10.54s per sample depending on activation precision, and requires $3.8\times$ fewer learning steps and $22\times$ less learning compute than quantized latent replay at higher accuracy and comparable latency.

papers.title: Mechanistic Critics for Sample-Efficient NPU Design-Space Exploration
papers.abstract: NPU design-space exploration for LLM inference mainly relies on an expensive simulator that often returns only scalar feedback such as latency and power. Such feedback can rank evaluated configurations, but gives little information for deciding why a configuration is slow or which architecture parameter should be changed next. This limitation is especially severe because prefill and decode workloads can be limited by different resources, including compute throughput and HBM bandwidth. We propose CriticNPU, a sample-efficient DSE framework built around an online-calibrated mechanistic critic for NPU architecture design. The critic uses explicit hardware limits to evaluate NPU configurations: before simulation, it estimates whether a proposed configuration is likely to improve over the current best and filters weak candidates; after simulation, it aggregates operator-level runtimes into prefill/decode bottleneck summaries and predicts the effect of candidate parameter changes. We instantiate the critic with a Roofline-style model that derives compute and memory limits from architecture parameters and calibrates per-operator-type effective limits using simulator observations. And CriticNPU combines this critic with a workload extractor and an architecture planner to propose configurations. Across six LLM workloads and 16 deployment configurations per model, CriticNPU achieves best-or-tied-best latency in 74% of prefill and 87.5% of decode settings while using roughly half the simulator calls of competitive DSE baselines. We conduct extensive ablation studies and detailed analyses to validate the effectiveness of our method from multiple perspectives. Our code is available at https://github.com/bruno686/CriticNPU.

papers.title: MicroAssert: Microarchitecture-Aware Structured Assertion Generation for CPU Verification
papers.abstract: Automatic assertion generation reduces manual verification effort, yet existing approaches struggle to capture microarchitectural behaviors and cross-region interactions in CPUs. We present MicroAssert, a microarchitecture-aware framework that identifies functional regions directly from RTL and generates local and composite assertions through structured contracts and deterministic verification primitives. Coverage-guided feedback further improves verification completeness by progressively expanding proof-relevant RTL coverage. Evaluated on five open-source RISC-V CPUs against three existing assertion generation approaches, MicroAssert achieves 100% syntax correctness and complete branch, statement, and toggle coverage, with an average proven rate of 74.82% and Proof Core coverage of 90.96%. Mutation testing further demonstrates its advantage, achieving an average error detection rate of 28.73%, 1.99 to 3.51 times higher than existing methods. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of microarchitecture-aware assertion generation.

papers.title: Compute Before You Digitize: ADC-less Mixed-Signal Processing for Scalable Cryogenic Qubit Readout
papers.abstract: We introduce DIRAC, an ADC-less in-cryostat qubit readout architecture that uses analog computing to redraw the analog-digital boundary. Directly operating on the front-end's analog output, passive complex mixers perform the equivalent of digital demodulation, ping-pong active-RC integrators average their outputs into down-sampled per-qubit traces, and a time-domain stage digitizes them, eliminating Nyquist-rate ADCs. A TX-RX co-design derives the mixers' local oscillators from the readout transmitter's baseband rather than per-tone PLLs. A per-line calibration flow trains the matched filter jointly with the neural network, improving fidelity and enabling low-bit-width, low-voltage digital processing. Designed in 22 nm FD-SOI and evaluated at 4 K on 1.12M experimental shots, DIRAC matches the fidelity of a floating-point (FP32) digital pipeline for readout windows down to 750 ns, at 31.6$\times$ and 238$\times$ lower energy than the fixed-point (FxP) and FP32 pipelines. It cuts the total 4 K power per physical qubit by 50.4% and 68.6% relative to FxP and room-temperature flex cables, respectively. At a fixed logical-qubit count and 4 K budget, this yields, against FxP, a code distance larger by 2 to 6 and a 1.6-7.3$\times$ (Willow) and 4.9-204$\times$ (SI1000, $p = 10^{-3}$) lower logical error rate.

papers.title: Towards Fair Resource Sharing in Agentic LLM Serving
papers.abstract: As LLM agents increasingly execute complex, multi-step tasks on shared inference infrastructure, resource contention across the end-to-end LLM serving stack causes severe and uneven slowdowns across agents. Existing agentic serving systems primarily optimize throughput and latency, with comparatively limited attention to fairness among concurrent agents. Although fairness has been studied in conventional LLM serving at the token and request levels, these approaches do not fully capture cumulative delays and stateful resource dependencies across successive LLM calls within an agent. Moreover, interference spans request routing, runtime scheduling, and hardware resources, making agent-level fairness challenging to define and optimize across an end-to-end serving stack. This paper presents a cross-layer framework to define agent-level fairness, attribute sources of unfairness, and optimize fairness while preserving throughput. To account for agents with widely varying execution demands, we build a theoretical foundation to define fairness using slowdown relative to standalone execution. Our empirical analysis reveals that routing, runtime scheduling, and hardware contention jointly determine fairness, with performance-oriented policies often leading to prolonged queuing delays. To optimize fairness, we introduce Duru, which monitors each agent's slowdown and uses this signal to guide admission and scheduling decisions across the router and runtime. Duru further alleviates starvation through admission exceptions and integrates slowdown-driven autoscaling to adhere to Service-Level Objectives (SLOs). Our evaluation across various benchmarks and hardware platforms shows that Duru reduces 99th-percentile normalized slowdown by a geometric mean of 44.4% (up to 79.5%) while delivering 91.8-127.4% of the state-of-the-art system's throughput.

papers.title: EEG2MCU: Sensing-to-Execution Co-Design for Wearable EEG Inference
papers.abstract: Wearable EEG inference is constrained not only by model size, but also by the channel-dependent sensing front end that must process high-dimensional inputs before compact downstream computation. We present EEG2MCU, a sensing-to-execution co-design framework that treats electrode count as a hardware design variable through task-aware montage selection. EEG2MCU retains a compact time-frequency representation and generates only the INT8 regions required by each first-layer tile, avoiding full input materialization. Halo reuse and access-aware placement across Flash, SRAM, and tightly coupled memory further reduce redundant generation and data movement. On a Cortex-M7 MCU, EEG2MCU reduces peak SRAM by 11.38x relative to the baseline, including a 1.71x reduction from the 62-to-19 electrode montage, while reducing latency by 2.57x and energy by 2.48x. It retains 94-96% of full-montage accuracy, demonstrating practical high-dimensional EEG inference under tight embedded-resource constraints.

papers.title: How to Turn an Attention Neural Network into an Interpretable Hard-Logic Predicate Circuit: Truth-Table Predicate Extraction and State-Machine Merging under Ship-of-Theseus Replacement
papers.abstract: We convert a trained attention network as a whole, attention included, into a hard-logic predicate circuit that runs in its place. Every unit of the circuit is a 0/1 predicate on tokens, and every map between predicates is a minimised truth table. Short tables, such as the product of a query code and a key code, are minimised exactly, and wide feature-to-feature transitions become implication rules by noise-tolerant minimisation. Blocks are replaced one at a time from the output down, in the manner of the Ship of Theseus, and after each replacement the remaining soft part re-adapts to the frozen circuit. Attention selection takes two forms, a row-wise comparison of integer scores (order selection) and a learned rule (rule selection). Both are fitted on the ordinary training set alone, and only on the examples that the teacher classifies correctly, so that the circuit imitates the teacher where the teacher is right. On TweetEval-emotion, the complete circuit of DistilGPT2 reaches a test gold accuracy of 66.5 $\pm$ 1.3% with order selection and 57.4 $\pm$ 2.5% with rule selection over three seeds, against 74.7% for the teacher and 64.0% for a bag of word pieces fitted on the same tweets, and that of BERT-base reaches 70.0 $\pm$ 0.5% with order selection and 63.7 $\pm$ 1.2% with rule selection against 77.8%. The circuit needs no multiplier and no weight traffic, and its exported hardware description reproduces it bit for bit. By a synthesis-based estimate it classifies one tweet in about 1-2 $\mu$s (DistilGPT2) and 3-5 $\mu$s (BERT) on an FPGA card and in 5-9 $\mu$s on a palm-sized board whose module draws 7.5-15 W, two to three orders of magnitude faster than the network on a GPU at batch 1 (measured, 0.9-2.6 ms for DistilGPT2 including an optimised CUDA-graph baseline), at a cost of 8.5 (DistilGPT2) and 8.6 (BERT) points of gold accuracy for the synthesised seed-0 circuits.

papers.title: A Runtime System for Mitigating Crossbar Port Contention on SM-Partitioned GPUs
papers.abstract: To avoid scheduling delays when running concurrent workloads on a GPU, Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) partitioning mechanisms such as CUDA Green Contexts restrict each workload to separate SMs. Despite this partitioning, concurrent workloads still significantly slow down latency-critical workloads, which recent studies attribute to shared L2 cache and memory contention. However, contention also occurs at the crossbar ports connecting each Graphics Processing Cluster (GPC) of SMs to the L2 cache, as all SMs in a GPC share one port. Green Contexts spread workloads across GPCs, placing concurrent workloads in the same GPCs and forcing latency-critical memory requests to queue behind background requests. Packing workloads into separate GPCs avoids this contention, but forces latency-critical memory requests through fewer ports, limiting memory bandwidth. Consequently, neither spreading nor packing is always faster across workloads and GPUs. Based on these observations, we present GPCPlace, a runtime system that dynamically selects between spreading and packing by profiling workloads on the target GPU to estimate both slowdowns, and hooks kernel launches in the CUDA driver to set SM masks without application modifications. Across 14 GPUs and 112 workload cases, GPCPlace speeds up latency-critical workloads by up to 1.15x on average and 2.38x maximum over Green Contexts without degrading throughput.

papers.title: Programmable Probabilistic Computer with 1,000,000 p-bits
papers.abstract: Many problems in physics and machine learning require sampling the collective states of large numbers of interacting variables. On modern graphics processors, repeated movement of interaction data between memory and compute units can limit how efficiently these calculations can scale. Here we demonstrate a programmable probabilistic computer with one million interacting probabilistic bits (p-bits) across 18 field-programmable gate arrays, sustaining $10^{12}$ probabilistic updates per second. Coupling weights remain beside the update circuits in on-chip memory, and only single-bit boundary states pass between devices. Experiments on three-dimensional and quasi-two-dimensional spin glasses show that the ratio of boundary-exchange frequency to local update frequency controls the effect of communication delays on optimization. A bound derived from the graph partition and interconnect identifies operating conditions that recover the residual-energy decay of an unpartitioned GPU reference. Infrequent exchange reduces the decay exponent, although faster local updates can shorten the time to reach a target energy. A cluster mean-field model reproduces this dependence, while ferromagnetic sampling experiments reveal a corresponding dependence of magnetization relaxation on the same frequency ratio. These results establish a million-p-bit computing architecture in which processing and local memory scale together, and provide a quantitative design principle for exploiting tolerance to communication delays in larger probabilistic computers.

papers.title: NAQsim: Full-Stack Architecture Simulation Framework for Fast and Space-Efficient Neutral Atom Quantum Computing
papers.abstract: Technological advances in neutral-atom platforms have opened a new path toward designing efficient protocols for fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC). However, each physical operation is still orders of magnitude slower than on other platforms, such as superconducting qubits. Therefore, architects must identify fast and efficient FTQC architectures, which require reliable modeling tools to explore various design choices across the software, classical hardware, and quantum device stacks of neutral-atom platforms. In this paper, we propose NAQsim, an open-source simulation framework for neutral-atom FTQC architectures based on transversal gates. As its key feature, NAQsim enables detailed full-stack architecture evaluation that opens opportunities to explore previously overlooked performance bottlenecks. As a first use case for NAQsim, we identify one such bottleneck, patch rotations, perform full-stack co-optimization, and finally derive a near-rotation-free architecture (D3-ROT). For practical FTQC benchmark workloads, D3-ROT achieves a 2.27x speedup from this single bottleneck alone, with minimal footprint overhead. These results point to a much broader space of full-stack optimizations that NAQsim makes accessible for transversal surface-code architectures and beyond.

papers.title: blaris: Windowless Random-Access LZSS for Constrained Microcontrollers
papers.abstract: Embedded LZ77 decompressors (such as heatshrink and tamp) require an in-RAM sliding window that couples memory usage to compression ratio and incurs high latency on random-access reads. We present blaris, a lightweight, windowless LZSS decompressor for execute-in-place (XIP) random access on constrained microcontrollers. By partitioning tokens into bidirectionally traversable streams with power-of-two checkpoints, blaris resolves back-references directly in the compressed payload, achieving compression ratios comparable to high-window heatshrink and tamp configurations without allocating a RAM window. Targeting compress-on-host, decompress-on-device workflows, blaris assumes trusted build-time payloads and omits runtime error and bounds checks. On RV32IMC, it requires just 548-784 B of Flash and 104-112 B of total RAM, achieving orders-of-magnitude faster small-slice random reads than ratio-matched, block-indexed heatshrink and tamp.

papers.title: RFAmpDesigner: A Two-Level LLM-guided Optimization Framework for Automated Differential CMOS RF Amplifier Sizing
papers.abstract: Automated RF amplifier sizing is challenging because the design process is inherently hierarchical, the parameter space is high-dimensional and strongly coupled, and high-fidelity circuit simulation is expensive. Conventional optimization and reinforcement learning methods typically require many iterations and make limited use of RF domain knowledge, making them costly under tight simulation budgets. Large language models (LLMs) provide broad prior knowledge and reasoning capabilities, but are unreliable for direct numerical optimization. This paper presents RFAmpDesigner, a two-level optimization framework for automated schematic-level sizing of differential CMOS RF amplifiers. At the outer level, the circuit-parameter space is abstracted into a resource-allocation space, where LLMs make high-level allocation decisions and adjust them according to feedback from the inner level. At the inner level, RF design knowledge is used to decompose the flat sizing problem into a sequence of low-dimensional subproblems. Conventional optimizers then solve these subproblems to find circuit implementations consistent with the assigned resources. This structure allows numerical optimizers to focus on low-dimensional searches in the circuit-parameter space, while the LLM reasons and acts over a physically meaningful design space using simulation feedback. The main evaluation covers low-noise amplifier (LNA), driver amplifier (DA), and power amplifier (PA) designs within the target differential CMOS RF amplifier family. Experimental results show that it achieves a higher success rate under a limited simulation budget in both easy and hard regimes.

papers.title: Contour: Extensible Mapping Surfaces for Agentic Accelerator Kernel Generation
papers.abstract: Emerging accelerators rarely ship with mature compiler backends, so recent work asks LLM agents to write native kernels directly from ISA documentation and simulator feedback. On two such accelerators, this direct workflow returns a correct kernel on only 17 of 38 workload instances, and most of its inference budget is spent re-deriving machine semantics and repairing illegal code rather than optimizing the workload. We present Contour, which consists of two parts. Contour-Explore replaces native-code generation with search over a mapping surface: a typed set of scheduling knobs and their legal domains, generated automatically from the accelerator's ISA description and the workload graph. A compiler-owned resolver completes partial assignments into legal plans and emits native code, so every evaluated candidate is verified against the compiler's default, and any policy can drive the search, including hill climbing, evolutionary search, and LLM agents. Compared with KernelCraft, a state-of-the-art agentic kernel generator, an LLM agent through Contour-Explore returns a verified kernel on every Gemmini and PLENA instance, produces 2.86x and 1.13x faster kernels on the instances where both succeed, and uses 26.3% and 83.4% fewer tokens per verified kernel. Contour-Ext extends the surface when search stalls: an LLM agent implements a new knob and its lowering in the compiler backend, and Contour-Ext accepts the extension only if the default path is byte-identical, every new value is numerically correct and changes the program, and the enlarged surface yields a measured gain. On VTA, Contour-Ext extends the AutoTVM surface of TVM, and AutoTVM's XGBTuner then finds 4.14x faster kernels; on PLENA, the extended surface makes the kernels found by hill climbing 1.20x faster.

papers.title: SPLASH: Co-Designing Flash-Aware Sparse Attention with a Virtualized HBM-HBF Hierarchy
papers.abstract: As context lengths, request lifetimes and concurrency grow, the key-value (KV) cache dominates memory usage in large language model (LLM) inference. High-bandwidth memory (HBM), the memory on contemporary GPUs, achieves far higher bandwidth than off-package memory, yet its capacity, bounded by DRAM density, has not kept pace with this demand. High-Bandwidth Flash (HBF), an emerging memory technology, bridges this gap, combining the advanced packaging of HBM with the density of flash to deliver terabyte-scale capacity at HBM-class read bandwidth. Exploiting this capacity for long-context KV caches, however, requires hiding the vastly different physical characteristics of flash from the GPU while keeping decode interactive. We therefore introduce Splash, an architecture that virtualizes HBM and HBF for the KV cache. We architect custom HBM and HBF base dies with novel memory and flash controllers that handle the access semantics and device management of flash. These controllers keep the GPU agnostic of the underlying memory, allowing the HBM-HBF hierarchy to behave as one logical memory for the KV cache. The added capacity of HBF enables long contexts, but dense attention, which reads the entire KV cache for every generated token, cannot keep decode interactive at these lengths. Splash therefore makes sparse attention flash-aware through query-driven address translation, in which the HBF base die resolves each query into the flash addresses of the relevant KV pages and schedules their reads across flash planes. Since the HBF base die holds the location of every page, this translation hides flash from the GPU and balances the selected reads across flash planes, coupling abstraction with performance. Across five models and up to one million tokens, Splash improves per-GPU decode throughput by up to 4.5x over the strongest baseline under a 100 ms latency budget.

papers.title: KatoANN: Enabling Near-Exact Vector Search at the Speed of Lossy Scans with CPU Matrix Engines
papers.abstract: Emerging CPU matrix engines, such as Intel AMX, enable high throughput by batching multiple queries. However, they support only low-precision formats, which can significantly degrade recall (i.e., search quality). We present KatoANN, the first approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search system that achieves both high throughput and high recall simultaneously on CPU matrix engines. Specifically, KatoANN represents each vector using a 16-bit code, splits it into high- and low-byte planes, and computes near-exact distances using 8-bit matrix multiplications that the matrix engine supports. To reduce extra multiplication overhead, it ranks all candidates by their high bytes alone and refines only a few survivors with the full distance. KatoANN also reduces memory footprint since it does not maintain a full-precision copy of the vectors. We implement a KatoANN prototype on Intel AMX. Our experimental results show that KatoANN outperforms existing partition-based systems across the high-recall range.

papers.title: Run, Read Back, Refine: Observation Fidelity in Execution-Grounded EDA Agents
papers.abstract: Design engineers lose the most time orchestrating flows and patching the gaps where closed EDA tools refuse to interoperate. We present an execution-grounded LLM agent for PyAether, SKILL, and Tcl that closes a generate-execute-refine loop over unified MCP tools (API retrieval, documentation, sandbox execution) and is already deployed in production EDA flows, with a grounding-gap framework positing that EDA-scripting correctness is bottlenecked by observation fidelity at the L4 (situated) layer, which model scale alone cannot reach. On EDA-Scripting-Bench (449 tasks, three languages, four commercial runtimes), the system reaches 76.5% pooled Pass@1 versus 19.7% (pure LLM): the system-level observation axis spans 56.8 percentage points with the model fixed, exceeding the 23.3-percentage-point backbone range with the harness fixed---two axes answering different questions; observation is an under-invested axis whose returns are measurable and graded.
